title: A quality rule needs a measurement and an explicit consequence
goal: Separate detecting bad rows from deciding whether to keep, drop, block, or notify so the product mechanism matches the publication risk.
tag: Focused certification lesson · data quality and governance · cycle 4, position 4
concept:
A scale can report that a package is overweight. It does not decide whether to label the package, remove one item, or stop the truck.

A data-quality rule has three parts: the condition, the measured result, and the consequence. Databricks Lakeflow expectations evaluate rows inside a pipeline and can warn, drop rows, or fail an update. Snowflake data metric functions run on a schedule and return measurements; expectations and notifications interpret those measurements. Monitoring alone does not rewrite or stop an unrelated load.
example: A 100-row orders batch contains four rows with a missing order_id. Warn keeps 100 and records four failures. Drop publishes 96. Fail-update publishes no new version. A scheduled Snowflake NULL_COUNT can report 4; a separate expectation such as “value = 0” marks a quality issue and can notify.

use_case.when: Use governed quality checks when a measurable defect has a named owner and a deliberate publication consequence.
use_case.example: A bronze orders feed may retain and count malformed rows, while the finance-ready table must fail publication when any order ID is missing.
use_case.decision: Warn while learning a baseline, drop only when losing invalid rows is acceptable and auditable, fail when partial publication is unsafe, and notify when asynchronous monitoring is the right control. Do not turn every anomaly into a pipeline outage.

practice: Move the invalid-row count and choose warn, drop, or fail. Predict published rows and recorded violations, then compare the product implementations.
boundary: The local model counts one null rule over one batch. It does not execute either platform, model streaming retries, pipeline graphs, event-log retention, DMF schedules, alerts, editions, permissions, costs, or downstream publication orchestration. Vendor SQL/Python was not run.

product_sections.title: Databricks: expectations sit inside the pipeline update
product_sections.html:
The rule travels with the transformation. Lakeflow expectations use SQL Boolean expressions on streaming tables, materialized views, or views. Default EXPECT retains invalid rows and records metrics. ON VIOLATION DROP ROW removes them. ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE fails the flow and atomically rolls back a table update.

-- sourced SQL sketch; not executedCONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL)  ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE

Failure/fix. In a triggered pipeline, one failed flow does not automatically fail independent parallel flows. Design the dependency/publication boundary explicitly. Metrics also have documented object/operator limits.

Execution label. SQL is an unexecuted vendor sketch. The row-flow view is local JavaScript.

product_sections.title: Snowflake: DMFs measure on a schedule; expectations interpret results
product_sections.html:
The monitor revisits the table. Associate a system or custom DMF with a table or view and set DATA_METRIC_SCHEDULE. The DMF returns a measurement such as null count, freshness, duplicates, or schema changes. An expectation defines which result is a problem; notifications can report violations. Data Quality Monitoring is documented as an Enterprise Edition feature.

-- sourced SQL sketch; not executedALTER TABLE PROD.ORDERS  ADD DATA METRIC FUNCTION SNOWFLAKE.CORE.NULL_COUNT  ON (ORDER_ID);

Failure/fix. A DMF result of four does not itself remove rows or undo the load. Bind an expectation, notification, and owner; add an orchestration gate separately when publication must stop.

title: Take completed results in finish order, not submission order
goal: Use ExecutorCompletionService when early completed work should be consumed without waiting behind an earlier slow task.
concept:
Three restaurant orders were placed A, B, C. B is ready first. Waiting at the counter for A before collecting B lets hot food go cold.

Keeping a list of Futures and calling get() in submission order can block behind slow A even when B and C are done. ExecutorCompletionService places each completed future onto a completion queue. take() returns the next finished task.
example: A takes 120 ms, B takes 20 ms, and C takes 60 ms. Submission-order reads produce A, B, C after A finishes. Completion-order reads produce B, C, A and let downstream processing start earlier.

use_case.when: Use completion order for independent fan-out calls whose results can be processed as each finishes.
use_case.example: Query three independent shard summaries and stream each ready result into an aggregation buffer.
use_case.decision: Keep submission order when output order is contractual. Use invokeAny for the first acceptable result, or structured-concurrency primitives when cancellation and task lifetime need a stronger scope.

practice: Change task durations and compare submission-order blocking with the completion queue's visible order.
boundary: The Java replay uses three sleeping tasks and a fixed pool. It does not measure scheduler precision, exceptions, timeouts, cancellation, bounded completion queues, structured concurrency, downstream ordering, or production latency.

title: Failover buys continuity; failback must reconcile the writes made while away
goal: Treat return-to-primary as a separate migration with reverse replication, consistency evidence, and another traffic decision.
concept:
Moving into a hotel during a home repair is not the same as moving home. The belongings acquired at the hotel must come back too.

After failover, the recovery region becomes the live source of truth. Failback requires rebuilding or validating the original region, replicating new writes back, proving the lag is within the RPO, then redirecting traffic. A tested failover button without a failback plan leaves the organization operating indefinitely in recovery mode.
example: Primary had 1,000 orders at failover. Recovery accepts 27 new orders. Redirecting traffic back before reverse synchronization exposes only 1,000. Replicate and validate first; then primary has 1,027 before the controlled cutback.

use_case.when: Design failback whenever regional recovery changes the authoritative write location or buffers regional messages.
use_case.example: An order API fails from us-east-1 to us-west-2, where Kafka and the database accept new writes for six hours.
use_case.decision: Remain in the recovery region until the primary is healthy, reverse replication is complete, in-flight messages are reconciled, dependencies are ready, and the business approves the second risk event. Do not rush back merely because the original region is reachable.

practice: Add recovery-region writes and toggle reverse synchronization. Watch the cutback expose a gap or a reconciled total.
boundary: The arithmetic model has one append-only count. It does not model conflicts, dual writes, message ordering, DNS caches, replication topology, RPO/RTO, data sovereignty, dependent services, or AWS DRS operations.

title: Use run hooks for the whole journey and agent hooks for one specialist
goal: Place lifecycle instrumentation at the scope that matches the question without mistaking observation for policy enforcement.
concept:
A trip recorder follows the whole journey across drivers. A coach's notebook follows only one driver.

OpenAI Agents SDK RunHooks observe an entire Runner.run, including agent changes and handoffs. AgentHooks attach to one agent. Both expose lifecycle callbacks around agents, model calls, tools, and handoffs. Hooks are good for metrics, logging, and prefetching; they are not automatically an authorization boundary or a durable transaction log.
example: A triage agent calls a tool, hands off to a refund agent, and the refund agent calls another tool. One run hook records both agents and both tools. Hooks attached only to refund record the refund start, its tool, and its end—not the triage events.

use_case.when: Use run hooks for end-to-end latency, usage and trace correlation; use agent hooks for specialist-specific metrics or setup.
use_case.example: Measure total support-run latency while separately tracking refund-agent tool failures and output quality.
use_case.decision: Prefer built-in tracing where it already answers the question. Add hooks for application-specific events, minimize sensitive payload capture, keep callbacks fast, and use guardrails/tool authorization for enforcement rather than relying on logging callbacks.

practice: Switch observer scope and step through triage, tool, handoff, refund, and tool events. Watch which events remain visible.
boundary: The local timeline does not run the SDK, callbacks, tracing, models, tools, sessions, concurrency, approvals, errors, or sensitive-data controls. It simplifies callback names and ordering for one successful path.

title: A nearby indirect state can slow recombination without giving up strong absorption
goal: Understand the reported pseudo-direct band structure in bismuth sulfide and why it is promising rather than a finished solar-cell result.
concept:
A busy station has a bright entrance and a quieter waiting room one level below. Light brings carriers in efficiently through the bright direct transition; many carriers spend time in the nearby indirect reservoir before recombining.

The study reports that bismuth sulfide has a lower-energy indirect transition and a strong direct transition only tens of meV above it. At room temperature, thermal exchange between the states preserves strong absorption while delaying bimolecular electron–hole recombination. For a reported splitting near 40 meV, modelling and measurements support about 75% suppression relative to the direct-only expectation.
example: The teaching model starts with 100 carrier pairs. A reservoir-share control moves carriers into a slower indirect state. At 75% modeled suppression, a toy interval shows 25 recombination opportunities instead of 100. This is a proportional intuition, not the paper's kinetics.

use_case.when: Use the result to guide research on solar absorbers, photocatalysis, and screening for materials with closely spaced direct and indirect transitions.
use_case.example: A materials team screens candidates for strong absorption plus longer carrier lifetime for multi-electron solar-fuel reactions.
use_case.decision: Treat Bi₂S₃ as a demonstrated pseudo-direct candidate, not a certified high-efficiency device. Device transport, traps, interfaces, stability, scalable films, extraction, toxicity and full-cell efficiency still need evidence.

practice: Move the suppression control and watch strong absorption remain while the toy recombination count falls. Compare that with an indirect material that sacrifices absorption.
boundary: The proportional model does not implement van Roosbroeck–Shockley theory, temperature dependence, band populations, traps, diffusion, extraction, spectra, device efficiency, or the paper's fitted kinetics. The 75% claim is scoped to the reported room-temperature analysis near ΔE≈40 meV.

title: Job outputs are small control messages, not an artifact transport
goal: Keep GitHub Actions job outputs bounded and non-secret; move large files through artifacts instead of the needs context.
concept:
A baggage tag tells the next worker which suitcase to fetch. It is not the suitcase.

GitHub job outputs pass small strings to dependent jobs through needs. GitHub documents a 1 MB maximum per job and 50 MB total per workflow run, approximated with UTF-16 encoding. Outputs that may contain secrets can be redacted and not sent. Large reports, binaries, and datasets belong in workflow artifacts.
example: A build job emits image_digest=sha256:… and artifact_name=service-linux as outputs. The 18-MB binary is uploaded as an artifact. The deploy job reads the two identifiers, downloads the artifact, and verifies the digest.

use_case.when: Use job outputs for small routing decisions, IDs, digests, versions, booleans, and artifact names needed by dependent jobs.
use_case.example: A matrix build returns one image digest per platform while artifacts carry SBOMs and test bundles.
use_case.decision: If downstream logic needs file contents, upload an artifact. If the value is sensitive, use the appropriate secret mechanism and minimize propagation. Treat output size limits as ceilings, not targets.

practice: Change payload size and secret-likeness. Watch the model select output, artifact, or blocked propagation.
boundary: The model approximates UTF-16 as two bytes per character and one job. GitHub's real approximation, masking heuristics, matrix-output behavior, artifact retention, permissions, compression, and billing are not executed.

title: Missing and null are different—and OpenAPI 3.1 spells null differently
goal: Model field presence separately from nullability and migrate schemas without silently rejecting or accepting the wrong payloads.
concept:
An empty delivery box is different from no box arriving. JSON null is a present field with no value; a missing property is absent.

In OpenAPI 3.0, a string that also accepts null uses type: string plus nullable: true. OpenAPI 3.1 aligns with JSON Schema and can use type: [string, 'null']. Separately, listing the property in the parent's required array controls whether it must be present.
example: middle_name may be absent when not collected, null when explicitly unknown, or a string when known. If it is required and nullable, absence fails but null passes. If optional and non-null, absence passes but null fails.

use_case.when: Make the distinction explicit during API schema design, SDK generation, database mapping, PATCH semantics, and OpenAPI 3.0-to-3.1 migration.
use_case.example: A customer profile distinguishes “producer did not send tax residency” from “customer explicitly has no secondary residency.”
use_case.decision: Allow null only when it has domain meaning. Prefer optional absence for fields not collected. Test generators and validators during version migration; do not mechanically leave 3.0-only nullable keywords in a 3.1 contract.

practice: Toggle required, nullable, and payload state. Predict validation before the result appears, then switch the displayed 3.0/3.1 schema form.
boundary: The validator models one property only. It does not execute an OpenAPI validator or generator, model PATCH merge semantics, defaults, oneOf, read/write direction, serialization, language option types, or every JSON Schema dialect.
